standard_text: Explain how opposite signs of numbers indicate locations on opposite sides of 0 on the number line; identify the opposite of the opposite of a number.

progression.narrative: 6.NS.2 asks students to understand integers as locations on a number line: a number and its opposite sit the same distance from 0 on opposite sides, and taking the opposite of an opposite returns the original number. The on-grade skills build from spotting opposite pairs on a drawn line, to naming a signed number from a distance and direction, to writing the opposite of any rational number, and finally to reasoning about the opposite of an opposite. Students who struggle here usually have a shaky number line underneath them: they cannot place a number by counting equal units from 0, or they cannot tell how far apart two points are. When the line itself is unfamiliar, the ideas of direction, distance, and same distance on opposite sides have nothing to stand on. Intervention rebuilds the number line and distance in grades 3 and 4, then the grade 5 work of locating rational numbers and reading positions in the coordinate plane, before returning to signed numbers and opposites.

steps.rationale: Opposites begin as a picture: mirror twins across 0. A plotted point lets the student count both checks -- opposite sides AND equal distance -- before any notation carries the load.
The standard says opposite signs indicate LOCATIONS. From 'N units left/right of 0' the student names the signed number and its opposite -- the first place distance and value must be kept separate.

The integer idea extends to all rational numbers: the opposite of a decimal or fraction changes only the sign. Here 'opposite' must be distinguished from 'reciprocal' before both words are needed later.
Understanding means saying it: any pair -N and N sits the same distance from 0 in opposite directions. This step dismantles 'smaller means closer to 0' -- the value-versus-distance confusion.

The standard's final clause: the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself. Treating each sign as a flip across 0 -- including for variables like -(-n) -- is the capstone of the progression.

skills.name: Locate and order whole numbers on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Place whole numbers on a number line by counting equal units from 0, and tell which of two numbers sits farther right.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: On a number line, is 8 to the left or the right of 5?

skills.i_do_script: A number line is a ruler for numbers. Watch: I start at 0, the home mark, and count equal jumps to the right, one unit per jump. To place 6, I count 6 jumps from 0 and make a point. Numbers grow as I move right, so 6 sits to the right of 4 and to the left of 9. I always count from 0, never from the end of the line.

canonical_error.pattern: Counts the marks instead of the spaces between them, or starts the count at 1 instead of 0
canonical_error.example: Places 6 at the seventh mark because the student counted the 0 mark as 1
canonical_error.why: A number line measures units, which are the gaps between marks. Counting the marks themselves, or starting the count at the first mark, shifts every point by one.

One equal step between two marks on the number line.

activities.instructions:

skills.name: Find the distance between two points on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Find how far apart two whole numbers are on a number line by counting the units between them or by subtracting.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: How many units apart are 3 and 7 on a number line?

skills.i_do_script: Distance on a number line is how many units apart two points are. Watch: to find the distance from 3 to 7, I count the jumps between them: 4 jumps, so the distance is 4. I can also subtract: 7 minus 3 is 4. Distance from 0 is quick, because the distance from 0 to 6 is just 6, the count of jumps from home. Distance is always counted as a positive amount, no matter which point I start from.

canonical_error.pattern: Counts the endpoints instead of the spaces between them, giving a distance one unit too big
canonical_error.example: Says 3 and 7 are 5 units apart by counting 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
canonical_error.why: Distance counts the gaps you jump across, not the numbers you land on. Counting both endpoints as jumps adds one extra unit.

skills.name: Locate positive fractions and decimals on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Place and compare positive fractions and decimals on a number line by their distance from 0.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Which is farther from 0 on a number line: 0.4 or 0.8?

skills.i_do_script: Fractions and decimals sit on the number line just like whole numbers, each at its own distance from 0. Watch: to place 0.8, I split the space from 0 to 1 into ten equal parts and count 8 parts to the right. To place 3/4, I split 0 to 1 into four parts and count 3. The bigger the number, the farther right it sits, so 0.8 is farther from 0 than 0.4. Every positive fraction and decimal has one home on the line, found by counting its distance from 0.

canonical_error.pattern: Orders decimals by how many digits they have instead of by place value, or places a fraction by its bottom number
canonical_error.example: Puts 0.35 farther from 0 than 0.5 because 35 is more than 5
canonical_error.why: More digits does not mean farther from 0. On the line, 0.5 is five tenths and 0.35 is three tenths and five hundredths, so 0.5 sits farther to the right.

skills.name: Plot points and read coordinates as distances from 0 in the first quadrant

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot ordered pairs in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane and read each coordinate as a distance from 0 along an axis.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot (3, 5), how far do you move from 0 along the bottom axis, and in which direction?

skills.i_do_script: A coordinate plane is two number lines that cross at 0, and that crossing point is the origin. Watch: to plot (3, 5), I start at the origin, move 3 units right along the bottom axis, then 5 units up along the side axis, and mark the point. The first number is the distance along the bottom, the second is the distance up. Each coordinate is just a distance from 0 in a direction, exactly like reading a point on a single number line.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the coordinates, moving up first or plotting (up, over) instead of (over, up)
canonical_error.example: Plots (3, 5) by moving 5 units right and 3 units up
canonical_error.why: The order in an ordered pair is fixed: the first number is the horizontal distance from 0, the second is the vertical distance. Swapping them lands on a different point.

redirect_script.praise: Over first, then up. Each number is a distance from 0 in its own direction.

vocabulary.definition: Two number lines that cross at 0, one going left to right and one going up and down.
The point where the two axes cross, at 0 on both. Its coordinates are (0, 0).

skills.name: Identify opposite numbers on a number line
skills.i_do_script: Opposites are mirror twins across 0. Watch me check whether −5 and 5 are opposites: I count −5's distance from 0 -- five units, on the left. Then 5's distance -- five units, on the right. Same distance, opposite sides: they're opposites. Two points are NOT opposites just because one is negative and one is positive -- the distances have to match.

canonical_error.pattern: Calls any negative-positive pair 'opposites' without checking that both are the same distance from 0
canonical_error.example: Says −3 and 5 are opposites because one is negative and one is positive
canonical_error.why: The student attends only to the signs. They haven't internalized that 'opposite' means a mirror image across 0 -- opposite signs AND equal distance from 0.

skills.item_template: A number line from −8 to 8 with labeled points. Student picks the pair of points that are opposites, or names the opposite of one marked point. MC with 4 choices; a figure is always shown.

sample_items.stem:

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from −8 to 8. Plot and label points: J at −5, K at −2, L at 1, M at 3, N at 5.
We're hunting for a pair of OPPOSITE points. Before we hunt -- what two things have to be true for two numbers to be opposites?
Look at K at −2 and M at 3. One is negative and one is positive. Are they opposites? Count each one's distance from 0.
If the student says K and M are opposites, they're using signs only. Have them count ticks: K is 2 from 0, M is 3 from 0. Ask: 'Do the distances match? Then can they be mirror twins?'
Now check J at −5. How far is J from 0? Which point on the RIGHT side is exactly that far from 0?
So which pair is the true opposite pair? Say the two checks that prove it.
Fold the number line at 0 (or draw a mirror arrow over the top). Show J landing exactly on N.
That's the test you'll run every time: opposite sides of 0, same distance from 0. Both checks, every time.

skills.name: Write the opposite of any rational number
skills.i_do_script: Opposites work the same for decimals and fractions as for integers: change ONLY the sign. Watch: the opposite of −3.8 is 3.8. The opposite of 5/6 is −5/6. I never touch the digits, never flip the fraction, never move the decimal point -- the number keeps its size and crosses to the other side of 0.

canonical_error.pattern: Flips the fraction (writes the reciprocal) instead of changing the sign
canonical_error.example: Says the opposite of 2/3 is 3/2 instead of −2/3
canonical_error.why: The word 'opposite' collides with 'flip it over' language students hear about reciprocals. They change the number's SIZE (turning it upside down) when opposite only ever changes the number's SIDE of 0.

skills.item_template: A single rational number (positive or negative decimal or fraction). Student writes its opposite. NR response. No computation beyond changing the sign.

sample_items.stem: What is the opposite of −3.8?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: −3.8 (no flip), 8.3 (digits reversed), 3.08 (decimal moved)

sample_items.stem: What is the opposite of 5/6?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 6/5 (reciprocal -- the canonical trap), −6/5 (reciprocal plus sign), 5/6 (no change)

sample_items.stem: What is the opposite of 12.4?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 12.4 (no change), 4.21 (digits shuffled), −4.12 (digits shuffled with sign)

sample_items.stem: What is the opposite of −2/5?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: −5/2 (reciprocal, sign kept), 5/2 (reciprocal with sign change), −2/5 (no change)

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- did the digits change, or just the sign?
redirect_script.prompt: The opposite changes ONE thing: the sign. Cover the sign with your finger -- everything you can still see must stay exactly the same. Now write the number with the other sign.
redirect_script.praise: Same digits, opposite sign. You didn't let 'opposite' turn into 'flip the fraction.'

vocabulary.definition: Any number that can be written as a fraction -- integers, decimals like 3.8, and fractions like 5/6.
The same number on the other side of 0 -- only the sign changes.
A fraction flipped upside down (2/3 becomes 3/2). This is NOT the opposite -- it changes the size, not the side.

skills.manipulative_visual: Write the number on a card in two parts: the sign on a small sticky note and the digits on the card. Taking the opposite = swapping only the sticky note. The card itself never changes.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS2-S4: explain in words where a number and its opposite sit on the number line.
next_steps.if_fail: Drop back to 6NS2-S2 with integers only, then reintroduce decimals first (they feel more like integers) and fractions last.

worked_example_script.text: Write two problems side by side: 'What is the opposite of −3.8?' and 'What is the opposite of 5/6?'
Before we touch these -- what did 'opposite' mean for integers? What changed, and what stayed the same?
Where does −3.8 live on a number line -- which side of 0, roughly how far? So where does its opposite live?
Write the opposite of −3.8. Did any digit change? Did the decimal point move?
Now 5/6. Some students write 6/5. What did they change about the number -- its sign, or its size?
If the student writes 6/5, they've reached for the reciprocal. Ask: 'Is 6/5 on the other side of 0 from 5/6? Both are positive! Which side of 0 should the opposite of a positive number be on?'
So what IS the opposite of 5/6? Say what changed and what stayed.
One rule for every rational number: the opposite keeps the digits and crosses 0. Flipping a fraction is a different move with a different name -- reciprocal -- and it belongs to a different job.

skills.i_do_script: Taking an opposite is a FLIP across 0. Watch what two flips do to −4: the opposite of −4 is 4 -- that's flip one. The opposite of 4 is −4 -- flip two, and I'm back where I started. So -(−4) means 'the opposite of −4,' which is 4 -- one flip. canonical_error.pattern: Reads -(-a) as 'still negative' -- treats each negative sign as a label meaning 'negative' instead of a flip across 0
canonical_error.example: Says -(−4) = −4, or says the opposite of the opposite of 7 is −7
canonical_error.why: The student sees a negative sign anywhere and concludes the answer is negative. They aren't tracking that each opposite is an ACTION (a flip across 0), so two flips cancel and return the original number.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: -(−4). Underneath, draw a number line from −5 to 5.

So -(−4) = 4. New question: what is the opposite of the OPPOSITE of −4 -- two flips this time. Flip from −4, then flip again. Where are you?

That's the rule the standard wants you to own: the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself. Signs aren't decorations -- each one is a flip, and two flips come home.

skills.name: Justify generalizations about opposites using variables and equations
skills.i_do_script: Up to now every opposite you took had a number attached. Now the number hides behind a letter. Here is the move that matters: -x does not mean 'a negative number.' It means 'the opposite of x.' If x is 5, then -x is −5. But if x is −5, then -x is 5 -- positive. The minus sign is an instruction to flip, and until you know which side x started on, you cannot say which side -x lands on.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads -x as 'a negative number' rather than 'the opposite of x', so any expression with a visible minus sign is judged negative regardless of what the variable holds
canonical_error.example: Says -x must be less than 0, or rules out -(-x) as an expression equal to x because 'it has minus signs in it'
canonical_error.why: For three years every minus sign the student met sat in front of an actual negative number, so sign and symbol always agreed. A letter breaks that agreement for the first time: the symbol says flip, and the value decides the direction.

skills.item_template: A generalization about opposites stated with variables -- an expression to evaluate for accuracy, a claim to judge, or a relationship to capture in an equation. Multi-select or constructed response; the reasoning is the answer, not the value.

sample_items.stem: A number line shows -b to the left of 0. Which expression represents the opposite of the opposite of -b?
sample_items.distractor_logic: b counts one flip; 0 treats the flips as cancelling the number away; -(-b) is one flip written out, not two.

sample_items.distractor_logic: The reciprocal options catch students who hear 'opposite' and reach for 'flip the fraction'; -x counts one flip.

sample_items.stem: Nonzero rational numbers r and t are opposites. Create an equation that describes the relationship between r and t.
sample_items.answer: r = -t (or t = -r, or r + t = 0, or any equivalent)
sample_items.distractor_logic: r = t misses the flip; r = 1/t confuses opposite with reciprocal; rt = 0 imports the wrong identity.

sample_items.stem: Jae says: 'If a number is written with a minus sign in front, it must be negative.' Is Jae right? Explain using a value for the variable.
sample_items.answer: No. -x means the opposite of x. If x = −6, then -x = 6, which is positive. The minus sign says flip, not negative.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Agreeing with Jae is the canonical error stated as a rule.

redirect_script.prompt: Try it twice. Let the letter be 5, and work it out. Now let the letter be −5, and work it out again. Did the answer land on the same side both times?
redirect_script.praise: You tested it instead of reading the sign off the page. That is what justifying a generalization looks like.

vocabulary.definition: A letter standing in for a number. It can hold a positive value, a negative value, or 0 unless you are told otherwise.
A claim meant to be true for every number, not just the one in front of you.
Show why a claim holds, with an equation, a number line, or a worked case -- not just assert it.
The flip of a fraction (the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2). Not the same as an opposite, and a common mix-up here.

next_steps.if_fail: Drop back to 6NS2-S5 and rebuild with numbers only, then reintroduce the letter by substituting one value at a time until the two cases are visible side by side.

worked_example_script.text: Write -x on the board. Below it draw a number line with 0 marked and a chip labeled x sitting to the right of 0.
Read -x out loud for me. Not 'negative x' -- what is it asking us to do to x?
x is sitting right of 0 here. If -x is the opposite of x, where does -x go? Point to it.
If the student says -x must be negative, do not correct it yet. Slide the chip to the LEFT of 0 and ask them to place -x again. Let the contradiction do the work.
Now x is left of 0. Where did -x land this time? Which side is it on?
So one minus sign, two different answers. What actually decided whether -x came out positive or negative?
The sign is an instruction to flip; the value of x decides the direction. That is why a claim about a letter has to be tested, not read off the page.

If x = 5, then -x = −5.  If x = −5, then -x = 5.
-(-x) = x -- two flips come home, whatever x holds.
r and t are opposites → r = -t, or r + t = 0.
Opposite flips the SIDE. Reciprocal flips the FRACTION. Different moves.

practice_problems.stem: Read Jae's claim. Decide whether it is correct and explain.

Jae's example: '-x has a minus sign, so -x is negative.'
practice_problems.answer: Jae is incorrect. -x means the opposite of x, not 'a negative number.' If x = −6, then -x = 6, which is positive. A counterexample is enough to sink the claim: one value of x where -x comes out positive proves the rule does not hold for every number.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error stated as a rule. A single counterexample is the whole justification -- students often try to argue in general when one case suffices.

practice_problems.stem: Is -(-m) always equal to m? Justify your answer for m positive, m negative, and m = 0.

practice_problems.stem: Sonia claims: 'p and q are opposites, so one of them has to be negative.' Is she right? Explain.

practice_problems.notes: Rewards precision about the domain of a generalization. The spec's own item says 'nonzero rational numbers' for exactly this reason.

activities.title: Sink the Claim
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair draws a claim card: '-x is always negative', '-(-x) = x', 'opposites always add to 0', 'if p and q are opposites, one is negative'.
2. Pairs decide true or false, then hunt for a single counterexample if false.
3. Rule: one counterexample sinks a claim, but no number of examples proves one -- a true claim needs a reason.
4. Pairs present. The class decides whether each defence was a reason or just more examples.

activities.title: Positive, Negative, or Depends
activities.instructions:
1. Show an expression: -x, -(-x), −5, -x when x < 0, x + (-x).
2. Students raise POSITIVE, NEGATIVE, or DEPENDS.
3. DEPENDS is the correct answer more often than students expect, and defending it requires naming two cases.
4. Any student who answers must give the value of x that backs their card.

strategy_links.why: Claims about letters are argued, not computed -- pairs have to defend a position and hear a counterexample from someone else.
The movable chip on the number line mat keeps the abstract claim tied to a position a student can point at.
Jae's rule is the canonical error written out as a generalization, which is exactly the form the above-proficiency items take.

questioning_prompts: Read -x out loud. What is it telling you to do to x?
Test it twice: let the letter be positive, then let it be negative. Same side both times?
You said always. What would a counterexample have to look like?
Can you write that relationship as an equation instead of a sentence?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student judges -x negative because of the visible minus sign.
misconception_redirects.say: Try it twice. Let the letter be 5, and work it out. Now let the letter be −5, and work it out again. Did the answer land on the same side both times?
misconception_redirects.praise: You tested it instead of reading the sign off the page. That is what justifying a generalization looks like.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student selects 1/x or −1/x as an expression for the opposite of x.
misconception_redirects.say: Opposite and reciprocal are two different flips. One crosses 0; the other turns the fraction over. Which one moves a number to the other side of 0?
misconception_redirects.praise: Right -- opposite changes the side, reciprocal changes the fraction.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student defends a general claim by listing more examples.
misconception_redirects.say: Those all work. But a claim says EVERY number. What reason covers the ones you didn't test?
misconception_redirects.praise: That's a reason, not a list. It covers numbers you never wrote down.

quick_checks.prompt: x = −7. Is -x positive or negative?
quick_checks.look_for: Positive, 7. 'Negative' means the sign is still being read as a label.

quick_checks.prompt: r and t are opposites. Give me an equation.
quick_checks.look_for: r = -t or r + t = 0. A blank means the relationship is understood in words but not yet in symbols.

worked_solution.stem: Nonzero rational numbers r and t are opposites. Create an equation that describes the relationship between r and t.

steps.annotation: Same distance from 0, on different sides.

check.prompt: Say what 'opposites' tells you about r and t.
check.answer: same distance from 0, on opposite sides

steps.math: So t is the opposite of r: t = -r.
steps.annotation: Write the relationship the way the sentence says it.

check.prompt: Write it as an equation. What does 't is the opposite of r' become?
check.answer: t = −r

steps.annotation: Taking the opposite of both sides says the same thing from r's point of view.
Opposites cancel. All three equations describe the same relationship.

check.prompt: Does r = −t force r to be negative? Why not?
check.answer: no -- −t means the opposite of t; if t is negative, r is positive

steps.math: So n is the opposite of m: n = −m.

steps.annotation: Name the Trap: write a third equation. Does m = −n force m to be negative?

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, write the opposite of any rational number, the At-proficiency core of the standard. If the student passes, move up to S5, the opposite of the opposite. If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks whether they can locate positive fractions and decimals on a number line, and B2 checks whether they can read a point as a distance from 0 in the coordinate plane, the grade 5 skills the opposite work rests on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (locate whole numbers on a number line) and F2 (distance between two points) find the gap in grades 3 and 4. S1, S2, and S4 stay available to probe the standard's own opposite-pair, distance-versus-sign, and location-language work.

pld_descriptors.note: Verbatim from the ILEARN item specification. These are performance bands on THIS standard, not lower-grade content: a student at Below Proficiency is working on this standard at its least complex entry point.
pld_descriptors.below: Identify or write the opposite of a given number with or without a given number line.
pld_descriptors.approaching: Plot 0 and/or the opposite of a given number on a number line, demonstrating the equal distances of opposites from 0 on either side of the number line.
pld_descriptors.at: Identify and/or write the opposite of the opposite of a given number. Reason about the opposite signs of numbers, their locations on a number line, and/or their absolute values to justify solutions.
pld_descriptors.above: Apply knowledge of the opposites of numbers to evaluate multiple expressions representing opposite relationships for accuracy, or interpret and make claims about given generalizations. Justify claims and generalizations using symbols, equations, and explanations.
